answer: Economics is the domain where the majority of authors tend to be male for both original and replication studies. Under the main specification (male-majority = authors_male > 0.5; originals counted at the O/R-pair id level, replications at the lab-row level, excluding drop=TRUE and aggregated=TRUE rows): 14 of 18 Economics original studies (0.778) and 13 of 18 Economics replication studies (0.722) have a male-majority author team. By contrast, Social sits at 37/64 originals (0.578) and 277/534 replications (0.519), and Cognitive at 33/49 originals (0.673) and 120/234 replications (0.513) — both only marginally above half for replications. No sensitivity specification (keeping drop=TRUE rows, including aggregated=TRUE rows, counting ties at exactly 0.5 as male-majority, or using the id-level replication unit) changes Economics as the winner; under ties-included it is even stronger (18/18 originals, 15/18 replications), and under the id-level replication unit it is the only domain with both proportions above 0.5 at all (0.778 / 0.722 vs Cognitive 0.673/0.449 and Social 0.578/0.484).

payload.hypothesis: In the Economics domain, the majority of authors tend to be male for both original and replication studies: 14 of 18 original studies (77.8%) and 13 of 18 replication studies (72.2%) have a male-majority author team (authors_male > 0.5). This contrasts with Social (57.8% of originals, 51.9% of replications male-majority) and Cognitive (67.3% of originals, 51.3% of replications), where the replication-side male-majority tendency is only marginal. The result is robust: Economics is the winning domain under every sensitivity specification tested (keeping drop=TRUE rows, including aggregated pooled replications, counting exact 0.5 ties as male-majority, and using an id-level replication unit).
payload.workflow: Loaded meta-regression_study_data_heterogeneity_in_replication_projects.csv (927 rows, 141 unique O/R-pair ids; the second CSV contains no author-gender or discipline fields and was used for context only). Verified zero missingness in id/discipline/authors_male.o/authors_male.r. Defined a study as male-majority when authors_male > 0.5 (strict; ties at 0.5 excluded from the numerator). Counted original studies at the id level (authors_male.o is constant within id) and replication studies at the lab-row level, excluding drop=TRUE and aggregated=TRUE pooled rows. Computed per-discipline proportions of male-majority originals and replications under the main spec and four sensitivity specs, and checked that no spec changes the winning domain.
